stem: The paper label on a tin of soup is a rectangle that is 23.5 cm long and 11 cm high. The label wraps exactly once round the tin and covers all of its curved surface. The tin is a cylinder.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the circumference of the tin.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the radius of the tin.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the volume of the tin.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The tin contains 425 cm\(^3\) of soup. Find the percentage of the volume of the tin that is filled with soup. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

idea: The curved surface of a cylinder unrolls into a rectangle. One side of the rectangle is the height of the cylinder, and the other side is the circumference of its circular end.

solution.label: a
steps: The long side of the label goes once round the tin, so it is the circumference.

solution.label: c
steps: The height of the tin is the height of the label, 11 cm.
\(V = \pi r^{2}h = \pi \times (3.740\ldots)^{2} \times 11 = 483.4\ldots\)
Keep the full value of \(r\) on your calculator. Do not type in the rounded 3.74.

solution.label: d
steps: \(\dfrac{425}{483.4\ldots} \times 100 = 87.91\ldots\)

stem: The ceiling of a planetarium is the inside of a hemisphere of diameter 18 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the area of the curved ceiling.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The ceiling is to be given two coats of paint. One litre of paint covers 8 m\(^2\), and the paint is sold in 10-litre tins. Find the number of tins that must be bought.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the volume of air under the ceiling, inside the hemisphere.

idea: A hemisphere is half of a sphere, so its curved surface area is half of \(4\pi r^{2}\) and its volume is half of \(\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}\). Start by halving the diameter to get the radius.

solution.label: a
steps: The radius is \(18 \div 2 = 9\) m.
Curved surface area \(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4\pi r^{2} = 2\pi \times 9^{2} = 508.9\ldots\)

solution.label: b
steps: Two coats cover \(2 \times 508.9\ldots = 1017.8\ldots\) m\(^2\), which needs \(1017.8\ldots \div 8 = 127.2\ldots\) litres.
\(127.2\ldots \div 10 = 12.7\ldots\) tins. Twelve tins are not enough, so round up.

solution.label: c
steps: \(V = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^{3} = \dfrac{2}{3}\pi \times 9^{3} = 1526.8\ldots\)

stem: The bowl of a glass is a cone with its point at the bottom. The top of the bowl is a circle of diameter 11 cm, and the bowl is 6 cm deep.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the volume of juice that the bowl holds when it is full.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Juice is poured in until it is 3 cm deep, which is half of the depth of the bowl. (i) Write down the radius of the surface of the juice. (ii) Find the volume of juice in the bowl.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the volume of the juice in part (b) as a percentage of the volume in part (a).

idea: The juice in a cone-shaped glass is itself a cone, with the same shape as the glass but smaller. When the depth is halved, the radius is halved too, so the volume falls by much more than half.

solution.label: a
steps: The radius is \(5.5\) cm.
\(V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^{2}h = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 5.5^{2} \times 6 = 190.0\ldots\)

solution.label: b
steps: (i) The juice makes a smaller cone of the same shape. Half the depth means half the radius: \(5.5 \div 2 = 2.75\) cm.
(ii) \(V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 2.75^{2} \times 3 = 23.75\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: \(\dfrac{23.75\ldots}{190.0\ldots} \times 100 = 12.5\)

This is \(\dfrac{1}{8}\). Halving both the radius and the height multiplies the volume by \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2}\). A glass that looks half full holds only one eighth of a full glass.

stem: Road salt is stored in a pile that has the shape of a cone. A worker measures round the edge of the base of the pile and finds that its circumference is 38 m. She also measures the distance from the edge of the base straight up the slope to the top of the pile. This distance is 8.5 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the radius of the base is 6.05 m, correct to three significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the vertical height of the pile.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the volume of salt in the pile.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A lorry can carry 20 m\(^3\) of salt. Find the least number of lorry loads needed to move the whole pile.

idea: The radius, the vertical height and the slant height of a cone form a right-angled triangle, with the slant height as the hypotenuse. The height of a pile cannot be measured directly, so it is found from the two lengths that can be.

solution.label: a
steps: This is 6.05 to three significant figures.

solution.label: b
steps: The distance up the slope, 8.5 m, is the slant height.

solution.label: c
steps: \(V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^{2}h = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi \times (6.0478\ldots)^{2} \times 5.972\ldots = 228.7\ldots\)

solution.label: d
steps: \(228.7\ldots \div 20 = 11.43\ldots\) Eleven loads would leave some salt behind, so round up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the length of the cylinder in the middle of the capsule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the volume of the capsule.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the surface area of the capsule.

idea: Split a compound solid into the simple solids it is made from. The two hemispheres here make one whole sphere. For the surface area, count only the faces on the outside: the flat ends of the cylinder are hidden inside the capsule.

solution.label: a
steps: Each hemisphere has radius \(3.5\) mm, so the two ends take up \(2 \times 3.5 = 7\) mm of the length.

solution.label: b
steps: Cylinder: \(\pi r^{2}h = \pi \times 3.5^{2} \times 14 = 538.7\ldots\)
Two hemispheres make one sphere: \(\dfrac{4}{3}\pi \times 3.5^{3} = 179.5\ldots\)
Total: \(538.7\ldots + 179.5\ldots = 718.3\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: Curved surface of the cylinder: \(2\pi rh = 2\pi \times 3.5 \times 14 = 307.8\ldots\)
Surface of the sphere made by the two ends: \(4\pi r^{2} = 4\pi \times 3.5^{2} = 153.9\ldots\)
Total: \(307.8\ldots + 153.9\ldots = 461.8\ldots\) The circular ends of the cylinder are not included, because they are inside the capsule.

stem: A weather balloon is a sphere. When it is released its diameter is 1.8 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the volume of the balloon when it is released.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The balloon expands as it rises. Find its diameter when its volume is 24 m\(^3\).

idea: The formula \(V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}\) connects the volume and the radius of a sphere. It can be used in either direction: put in \(r\) to get \(V\), or put in \(V\) and solve for \(r\).

solution.label: a
steps: The radius is \(0.9\) m.

solution.label: b
steps: Take the cube root: \(r = 1.789\ldots\)
The question asks for the diameter: \(2 \times 1.789\ldots = 3.578\ldots\)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the total area of glass in the four triangular faces.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the vertical height of the pyramid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the volume of the pyramid.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the length of the sloping edge [VA].

idea: A right pyramid contains several right-angled triangles. One joins the apex, the centre of the base and the midpoint of a side. Another joins the apex, the midpoint of a side and a corner. Choose the triangle that contains the length you want.

solution.label: a
steps: Each face is a triangle with base 36 m and height \(\mathrm{VM} = 30\) m: area \(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 36 \times 30 = 540\).

solution.label: b
steps: Let O be the centre of the base. Then \(\mathrm{OM} = 18\) m, half of the side, and triangle VOM has a right angle at O.

solution.label: c
steps: \(V = \dfrac{1}{3} \times \text{base area} \times \text{height} = \dfrac{1}{3} \times 36^{2} \times 24 = 10\,368\)
solution.answer: 10 368 m\(^3\) (10 400 m\(^3\) to three significant figures)

solution.label: d
steps: Triangle VMA has a right angle at M, with \(\mathrm{VM} = 30\) and \(\mathrm{MA} = 18\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use similar triangles to show that the height of the cone that has been removed is 48 cm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the volume of the bucket.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write down the volume of the bucket in litres.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Water is poured into the bucket until it is 12 cm deep, which is half of the depth of the bucket. (i) Write down the radius of the surface of the water. (ii) Find the volume of water in the bucket.

idea: A shape like a bucket is what is left when the tip is cut off a cone. Its volume is the volume of the whole cone minus the volume of the tip. The two cones have the same shape, so their measurements are in the same ratio.

solution.label: a
steps: Let the removed cone have height \(h\) cm. The whole cone then has height \(h + 24\) cm.
The two cones are similar, so radius \(\div\) height is the same for both: \(\dfrac{10}{h} = \dfrac{15}{h + 24}\).

solution.label: b
steps: The whole cone has radius 15 cm and height \(48 + 24 = 72\) cm: \(\dfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 15^{2} \times 72 = 16\,964.6\ldots\)
The removed cone has radius 10 cm and height 48 cm: \(\dfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 10^{2} \times 48 = 5026.5\ldots\)

solution.label: d
steps: (i) The radius grows steadily from 10 cm at the base to 15 cm at the top. Halfway up it is \(12.5\) cm.
(ii) The water, together with the removed tip, makes a cone of radius 12.5 cm and height \(48 + 12 = 60\) cm: \(\dfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 12.5^{2} \times 60 = 9817.4\ldots\)
Take away the tip: \(9817.4\ldots - 5026.5\ldots = 4790.9\ldots\)
This is about 40 % of the bucket, not 50 %, because the bucket is narrower at the bottom.

stem: A jug is a cylinder with internal radius 5 cm and height 13.5 cm. It stands on a table and contains water to a depth of 8 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the volume of water in the jug.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Glass marbles are spheres of radius 0.8 cm. Find the volume of one marble.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Forty marbles are dropped into the jug and sink to the bottom. Find the new depth of the water.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The marbles are taken out, so the depth is 8 cm again. A solid metal cone with base radius 4 cm is lowered into the jug until it is completely under water. The depth of the water rises by 1.6 cm. Find the height of the cone.

parts.label: e
parts.text: The cone is taken out. Find the greatest number of marbles that can be put into the jug before water spills over the top.

idea: An object that is completely under water pushes aside its own volume of water. In a cylinder, that extra volume appears as a thin cylinder of water on top, so the rise in the water level is the volume of the object divided by the area of the base of the jug.

solution.label: a
steps: \(V = \pi r^{2}h = \pi \times 5^{2} \times 8 = 628.3\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: Forty marbles have volume \(40 \times 2.144\ldots = 85.78\ldots\) cm\(^3\).
The base of the jug has area \(\pi \times 5^{2} = 25\pi\) cm\(^2\), so the water rises by \(\dfrac{85.78\ldots}{25\pi} = 1.092\ldots\) cm.
New depth: \(8 + 1.092\ldots = 9.092\ldots\)

solution.label: d
steps: The cone pushes aside a layer of water 1.6 cm deep: volume \(= 25\pi \times 1.6 = 40\pi\) cm\(^3\). This is the volume of the cone.
\(\dfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 4^{2} \times h = 40\pi\), so \(\dfrac{16}{3}h = 40\) and \(h = 7.5\).

solution.label: e
steps: The water can rise by \(13.5 - 8 = 5.5\) cm. That is a volume of \(25\pi \times 5.5 = 431.9\ldots\) cm\(^3\).
\(431.9\ldots \div 2.144\ldots = 201.4\ldots\) marbles. With 201 marbles the water is just below the top, and one more makes it spill.

stem: In a computer game, the position of each object is given by coordinates \((x,\,y,\,z)\), measured in metres, where \(z\) is the height above the ground. A ship is at \(\mathrm{A}(10,\,20,\,30)\). The point \(\mathrm{M}(30,\,50,\,45)\) is the midpoint of the line segment joining A to a second ship, B.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the coordinates of B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the distance between the two ships.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A third ship is at \(\mathrm{C}(30,\,60,\,25)\). Show that triangle ABC is isosceles.

idea: The midpoint is halfway along in each of the three directions, so going from A to M and then the same again reaches B. The distance between two points in three dimensions is Pythagoras with three differences instead of two: \(\sqrt{(\Delta x)^{2} + (\Delta y)^{2} + (\Delta z)^{2}}\).

solution.label: a
steps: From A to M the coordinates change by \(+20\), \(+30\) and \(+15\).
Make the same changes again, starting from M: \((30 + 20,\ 50 + 30,\ 45 + 15)\).

solution.label: c
steps: Two sides are equal, and the third side, \(\mathrm{AB} = 78.1\) m, is different.
solution.answer: \(\mathrm{AC} = \mathrm{BC} = 45\) m, so the triangle is isosceles

parts.label: d
parts.text: M is the midpoint of [AB] and N is the midpoint of [BC]. By finding the angles that [VM] and [VN] make with the horizontal, determine which is steeper: the roof face VAB or the roof face VBC.

idea: To find the angle between a sloping line and a horizontal plane, drop a vertical line from the top of the sloping line to the plane. This makes a right-angled triangle, and the angle you want is at the bottom of the sloping line.

solution.label: a
steps: The diagonal of the rectangle is \(\mathrm{AC} = \sqrt{12^{2} + 8^{2}} = \sqrt{208}\).
O is the midpoint of the diagonal: \(\mathrm{OA} = \dfrac{\sqrt{208}}{2} = 7.211\ldots\)

solution.label: b
steps: Triangle VOA has a right angle at O: \(\mathrm{VA} = \sqrt{3^{2} + (7.211\ldots)^{2}} = \sqrt{61} = 7.810\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: The angle is \(\mathrm{V\hat{A}O}\), in the same triangle. Opposite is \(\mathrm{VO} = 3\) and adjacent is \(\mathrm{OA} = 7.211\ldots\)
\(\tan(\mathrm{V\hat{A}O}) = \dfrac{3}{7.211\ldots}\), so the angle is \(22.58\ldots^\circ\)

solution.label: d
steps: M is 4 m from O, half of BC. In triangle VOM, \(\tan(\mathrm{V\hat{M}O}) = \dfrac{3}{4}\), so the angle is \(36.86\ldots^\circ\)
N is 6 m from O, half of AB. In triangle VON, \(\tan(\mathrm{V\hat{N}O}) = \dfrac{3}{6}\), so the angle is \(26.56\ldots^\circ\)
Both lines rise 3 m, but [VM] does it over a shorter horizontal distance.
solution.answer: \(36.9^\circ\) and \(26.6^\circ\), so the face VAB is steeper

stem: In a theatre, positions are given by coordinates \((x,\,y,\,z)\) in metres, where the stage floor is the plane \(z = 0\). A spotlight is fixed at \(\mathrm{S}(0,\,0,\,12)\). It shines on an actor who is standing on the stage at \(\mathrm{P}(5,\,12,\,0)\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The point \(\mathrm{F}(0,\,0,\,0)\) is on the stage floor, directly below S. Find the distance FP.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the length of the beam of light, SP.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the angle of depression of P from S.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The actor walks to \(\mathrm{Q}(9,\,12,\,0)\) and the spotlight follows her. Find the angle \(\mathrm{P\hat{S}Q}\) through which the beam turns.

idea: Break a three-dimensional problem into flat triangles. The light, the point below it and the actor make a right-angled triangle standing on the stage. The light and the actor's two positions make a second triangle, which has no right angle, so it needs the cosine rule.

solution.label: a
steps: F and P are both on the floor: \(\mathrm{FP} = \sqrt{5^{2} + 12^{2}} = 13\)

solution.label: b
steps: Triangle SFP has a right angle at F, with \(\mathrm{SF} = 12\) and \(\mathrm{FP} = 13\).

solution.label: c
steps: The angle of depression is measured down from the horizontal at S. It equals the angle \(\mathrm{S\hat{P}F}\) at the actor, because the horizontal at S is parallel to the floor.
\(\tan(\mathrm{S\hat{P}F}) = \dfrac{12}{13}\), so the angle is \(42.70\ldots^\circ\)

solution.label: d
steps: Cosine rule in triangle PSQ: \(\cos(\mathrm{P\hat{S}Q}) = \dfrac{\mathrm{SP}^{2} + \mathrm{SQ}^{2} - \mathrm{PQ}^{2}}{2 \times \mathrm{SP} \times \mathrm{SQ}} = \dfrac{313 + 369 - 16}{2\sqrt{313}\sqrt{369}} = 0.9798\ldots\)
\(\mathrm{P\hat{S}Q} = \cos^{-1}(0.9798\ldots) = 11.52\ldots^\circ\)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the angle that [AC] makes with the ground.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Explain why the answer to part (d) is smaller than the answer to part (b).

idea: The angle between a line and the ground is found in a right-angled triangle that has the line as its hypotenuse and the height gained as one of its sides. Two lines that climb to the same height can be at different angles, because the longer line gains the same height over a greater distance.

solution.label: a
steps: Triangle BFC has a right angle at F: \(\mathrm{BC} = \sqrt{3.5^{2} + 1.2^{2}} = \sqrt{13.69} = 3.7\)

solution.label: b
steps: The angle is \(\mathrm{C\hat{B}F}\): \(\tan(\mathrm{C\hat{B}F}) = \dfrac{1.2}{3.5}\), so the angle is \(18.92\ldots^\circ\)

solution.label: c
steps: ABCD is a rectangle, so triangle ABC has a right angle at B.

solution.label: d
steps: C is 1.2 m above the point F on the ground, so triangle AFC has a right angle at F and hypotenuse AC.
\(\sin(\mathrm{C\hat{A}F}) = \dfrac{\mathrm{CF}}{\mathrm{AC}} = \dfrac{1.2}{6.220\ldots} = 0.1929\ldots\)
\(\mathrm{C\hat{A}F} = 11.12\ldots^\circ\)

solution.label: e
steps: Both paths climb the same 1.2 m. The path from A to C is longer (6.22 m compared with 3.7 m), so it gains that height more gradually.
solution.answer: [AC] rises the same 1.2 m as [BC] but over a longer distance, so it is less steep

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fly travels in a straight line through the air from A to G. Find the distance AG.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the angle that [AG] makes with the floor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the length of the straight line from A to G on the flat drawing.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The spider could cross the edge [BC] instead, and then walk up the wall BCGF. By drawing this wall folded flat next to the floor, find the length of the shortest route of this kind.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Write down the length of the shorter of the two routes in parts (c) and (d).

idea: A path across the surfaces of a box is hard to see in three dimensions. Unfold the surfaces so that they lie flat: the shortest path on the surface then becomes a straight line on the flat drawing, and Pythagoras gives its length.

solution.label: b
steps: C is on the floor directly below G, so triangle ACG has a right angle at C. \(\mathrm{AC} = \sqrt{5^{2} + 4^{2}} = \sqrt{41}\) and \(\mathrm{CG} = 3\).
\(\tan(\mathrm{G\hat{A}C}) = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{41}}\), so the angle is \(25.10\ldots^\circ\)

solution.label: c
steps: On the flat drawing, G is 5 m across from A and \(4 + 3 = 7\) m up.

solution.label: d
steps: Fold the wall BCGF down so that it lies flat to the right of the floor, joined along [BC]. Now G is \(5 + 3 = 8\) m across from A and 4 m up.

solution.label: e
steps: Compare the two routes: 8.60 m is less than 8.94 m. Both are longer than the fly's 7.07 m, as they must be.

stem: Amara is flying a kite on a string of length 40 m. The string is straight and makes an angle of \(52^\circ\) with the horizontal. Her hand is 1.5 m above the ground.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the height of the kite above Amara's hand.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down the height of the kite above the ground.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The wind drops, and the string now makes an angle of \(35^\circ\) with the horizontal. The length of the string is still 40 m. Find the new height of the kite above the ground.

idea: The string is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle, and the height of the kite above the hand is the side opposite the angle. Opposite and hypotenuse are linked by sine.

solution.label: a
steps: \(\sin 52^\circ = \dfrac{\text{height}}{40}\), so height \(= 40\sin 52^\circ = 31.52\ldots\)

solution.label: b
steps: Add the height of her hand: \(31.52\ldots + 1.5 = 33.02\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: \(40\sin 35^\circ = 22.94\ldots\) m above her hand.

stem: An escalator in a shopping centre is 14 m long and carries people up to a floor that is 6.3 m higher.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the angle that the escalator makes with the horizontal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the horizontal distance between the bottom and the top of the escalator.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A second escalator rises through the same height at an angle of \(30^\circ\) to the horizontal. Find its length.

idea: Draw the right-angled triangle first. The escalator is the hypotenuse, the rise is the vertical side and the distance along the floor is the horizontal side. Then pick the ratio that links the two sides you know to the thing you want.

solution.label: a
steps: The rise, 6.3 m, is opposite the angle and the escalator, 14 m, is the hypotenuse.

stem: A tree stands on level ground. When the angle of elevation of the sun is \(40^\circ\), the shadow of the tree is 9.5 m long.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the height of the tree.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Later in the day the shadow is 5.5 m long. Find the angle of elevation of the sun at this time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the length of the shadow when the angle of elevation of the sun is \(60^\circ\).

idea: The tree, its shadow and the ray of sunlight that passes the top of the tree make a right-angled triangle. The tree is opposite the angle of elevation and the shadow is adjacent to it, so the ratio to use is tangent.

solution.label: a
steps: \(\tan 40^\circ = \dfrac{h}{9.5}\), so \(h = 9.5\tan 40^\circ = 7.971\ldots\)

solution.label: b
steps: \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{7.971\ldots}{5.5} = 1.449\ldots\)
\(\theta = \tan^{-1}(1.449\ldots) = 55.39\ldots^\circ\) A shorter shadow means that the sun is higher.

solution.label: c
steps: \(\tan 60^\circ = \dfrac{7.971\ldots}{s}\), so \(s = \dfrac{7.971\ldots}{\tan 60^\circ} = 4.602\ldots\)

parts.text: Find the width of the river, AT.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the distance BT.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Back at A, she measures the angle of elevation of the top of the tree as \(11^\circ\). Her eyes are 1.6 m above the ground, and the ground on both banks is at the same level. Find the height of the tree.

idea: A distance that cannot be measured directly can be found from one length and one angle that can. Here two right-angled triangles share the side AT: one lies flat on the ground and gives the width, and the other stands upright and gives the height.

solution.label: a
steps: Triangle ABT has a right angle at A. AT is opposite the \(63^\circ\) angle and AB is adjacent to it.
\(\mathrm{AT} = 40\tan 63^\circ = 78.50\ldots\)

solution.label: b
steps: \(\cos 63^\circ = \dfrac{40}{\mathrm{BT}}\), so \(\mathrm{BT} = \dfrac{40}{\cos 63^\circ} = 88.10\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: Now use an upright triangle. Its horizontal side is the width of the river, \(78.50\ldots\) m, and its angle at her eyes is \(11^\circ\).
Height of the top of the tree above her eyes: \(78.50\ldots \times \tan 11^\circ = 15.25\ldots\)
Add the height of her eyes: \(15.25\ldots + 1.6 = 16.85\ldots\)

idea: The horizontal line through the window splits the picture into two right-angled triangles, one above the line and one below it. They share the horizontal side. Work in the lower triangle first, because it contains the one length that is given.

solution.label: a
steps: In the lower triangle the vertical side is 12 m, opposite the \(28^\circ\) angle, and the horizontal side is the distance \(d\) between the buildings.
\(\tan 28^\circ = \dfrac{12}{d}\), so \(d = \dfrac{12}{\tan 28^\circ} = 22.56\ldots\)

solution.label: b
steps: In the upper triangle, the height of T above the window is \(22.56\ldots \times \tan 41^\circ = 19.61\ldots\) m.
Add the height of the window above the ground: \(19.61\ldots + 12 = 31.61\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: WT is the hypotenuse of the upper triangle: \(\cos 41^\circ = \dfrac{22.56\ldots}{\mathrm{WT}}\).
\(\mathrm{WT} = \dfrac{22.56\ldots}{\cos 41^\circ} = 29.90\ldots\)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the height of the top of the frame above the ground.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The instructions say that the angle between the legs should be \(35^\circ\). Find the distance between the feet when the angle between the legs is \(35^\circ\).

idea: An isosceles triangle has a line of symmetry from the top corner to the middle of the base. This line cuts the triangle into two equal right-angled triangles, each with half of the base and half of the top angle.

solution.label: a
steps: Draw the line of symmetry. Each right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 2.4 m and a side of \(1.3 \div 2 = 0.65\) m opposite the half-angle.
\(\sin(\text{half-angle}) = \dfrac{0.65}{2.4}\), so the half-angle is \(15.71\ldots^\circ\)
Double it: \(2 \times 15.71\ldots = 31.42\ldots^\circ\)

solution.label: b
steps: The height is the third side of the same right-angled triangle: \(\sqrt{2.4^{2} - 0.65^{2}} = 2.310\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: The half-angle is now \(17.5^\circ\). Half of the distance between the feet is \(2.4\sin 17.5^\circ = 0.7216\ldots\) m.
\(2 \times 0.7216\ldots = 1.443\ldots\)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the size of angle \(\mathrm{A\hat{O}B}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the length OM.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the area of the floor.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the length OA.

parts.label: e
parts.text: The floor is cut from a square sheet of wood. Four of the sides of the octagon lie along the four sides of the square. Find the percentage of the sheet that is cut away.

idea: Lines from the centre of a regular polygon to its corners cut it into equal isosceles triangles. Each of these splits into two right-angled triangles, so one right-angled triangle is enough to find every length in the polygon.

solution.label: a
steps: Eight equal angles meet at O: \(360^\circ \div 8\).

solution.label: b
steps: Triangle OMB has a right angle at M, angle \(\mathrm{M\hat{O}B} = 22.5^\circ\) and \(\mathrm{MB} = 1.25\) m.
\(\tan 22.5^\circ = \dfrac{1.25}{\mathrm{OM}}\), so \(\mathrm{OM} = \dfrac{1.25}{\tan 22.5^\circ} = 3.017\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: Triangle OAB has base 2.5 m and height OM: area \(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2.5 \times 3.017\ldots = 3.772\ldots\) m\(^2\).
The floor is eight of these: \(8 \times 3.772\ldots = 30.17\ldots\)

solution.label: d
steps: In triangle OMB, OB is the hypotenuse: \(\sin 22.5^\circ = \dfrac{1.25}{\mathrm{OB}}\), and \(\mathrm{OA} = \mathrm{OB}\).
\(\mathrm{OA} = \dfrac{1.25}{\sin 22.5^\circ} = 3.266\ldots\)

solution.label: e
steps: The square reaches from one side of the octagon to the opposite side, so its side is \(2 \times \mathrm{OM} = 6.035\ldots\) m and its area is \(36.42\ldots\) m\(^2\).
\(\dfrac{6.25}{36.42\ldots} \times 100 = 17.15\ldots\)

The furthest point on the sea that can be seen from L is the horizon, H. The line of sight [LH] touches the surface of the Earth at H, so it is perpendicular to the radius [OH].

parts.text: Write down the length OL, in kilometres.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the distance LH is 22.6 km, correct to three significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the angle \(\mathrm{L\hat{O}H}\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: A sailor's eyes are 15 m above sea level. Find the greatest distance from the lamp at which the sailor can see it.

idea: A line that touches a circle meets the radius at a right angle. So the centre of the Earth, the horizon and the observer make a right-angled triangle, even though two of its sides are thousands of kilometres long and the third is only a few kilometres.

solution.label: a
steps: \(40\) m \(= 0.04\) km. L is this far above the surface: \(6371 + 0.04\).

solution.label: b
steps: Triangle OHL has a right angle at H, with hypotenuse \(\mathrm{OL} = 6371.04\) and \(\mathrm{OH} = 6371\).
\(\mathrm{LH} = \sqrt{509.68\ldots} = 22.57\ldots\), which is 22.6 to three significant figures.

solution.label: c
steps: In triangle OHL, LH is opposite the angle at O and OH is adjacent to it: \(\tan(\mathrm{L\hat{O}H}) = \dfrac{\mathrm{LH}}{\mathrm{OH}} = \dfrac{22.57\ldots}{6371}\)
\(\mathrm{L\hat{O}H} = 0.2030\ldots^\circ\) The angle is tiny, because 22.6 km is very small compared with the radius of the Earth.
Tangent is the safest ratio here. The cosine of this angle is \(\dfrac{6371}{6371.04}\), which is so close to 1 that rounding it at all gives a wrong angle.

solution.label: d
steps: The sailor has a horizon too. Its distance from the sailor is found in the same way, with a height of 0.015 km: \(\sqrt{6371.015^{2} - 6371^{2}} = \sqrt{191.13\ldots} = 13.82\ldots\) km.
The sailor is at the greatest distance when the lamp and the sailor are on opposite sides of the same horizon point, so that the line of sight just touches the sea between them.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the length PQ.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the height of P above the beam [QR].

idea: When two angles and one side of a triangle are known, find the third angle and then use the sine rule: each side divided by the sine of the angle opposite it gives the same number.

solution.label: b
steps: PQ is opposite the angle at R, \(46^\circ\). QR is opposite the angle at P, \(102^\circ\).
Sine rule: \(\dfrac{\mathrm{PQ}}{\sin 46^\circ} = \dfrac{9.6}{\sin 102^\circ}\)
\(\mathrm{PQ} = \dfrac{9.6\sin 46^\circ}{\sin 102^\circ} = 7.059\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: Draw a vertical line from P down to the beam. It makes a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse PQ and an angle of \(32^\circ\) at Q.
Height \(= 7.059\ldots \times \sin 32^\circ = 3.741\ldots\)

stem: A ferry leaves a port P and sails 18 km in a straight line on a bearing of \(072^\circ\) to an island Q.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find how far Q is to the east of P.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find how far Q is to the north of P.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the bearing of P from Q.

idea: A bearing is an angle measured clockwise from north. Draw the north line at the starting point, and the journey becomes the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle whose other sides point north and east.

solution.label: a
steps: The \(72^\circ\) angle is between the north line and the path. The distance east is opposite this angle.
\(18\sin 72^\circ = 17.11\ldots\)

solution.label: b
steps: The distance north is adjacent to the angle: \(18\cos 72^\circ = 5.562\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: The journey back is in exactly the opposite direction, which is a half-turn from the first bearing.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find how far the aircraft is to the north of the coast.

idea: Bearings are measured from north, but the sine rule needs the angles inside the triangle. Turn each bearing into an inside angle first, using the fact that the line AB runs east to west, at \(90^\circ\) to each north line.

solution.label: a
steps: At A, east is \(90^\circ\) from north, and AP is \(55^\circ\) from north: \(\mathrm{P\hat{A}B} = 90^\circ - 55^\circ = 35^\circ\).
At B, the direction to A is west, a bearing of \(270^\circ\). BP is on a bearing of \(310^\circ\): \(\mathrm{P\hat{B}A} = 310^\circ - 270^\circ = 40^\circ\).

solution.label: c
steps: AP is opposite the \(40^\circ\) angle and AB is opposite the \(105^\circ\) angle.
Sine rule: \(\dfrac{\mathrm{AP}}{\sin 40^\circ} = \dfrac{80}{\sin 105^\circ}\)
\(\mathrm{AP} = \dfrac{80\sin 40^\circ}{\sin 105^\circ} = 53.23\ldots\)

solution.label: d
steps: Draw a line from P straight down to the coast. It makes a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse AP and angle \(35^\circ\) at A.
\(53.23\ldots \times \sin 35^\circ = 30.53\ldots\)

parts.text: Find the length of the tree, BT.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the vertical height of T above the ground.

idea: A leaning tree does not make a right angle with the ground, so the triangle formed by the tree, its shadow and the ray of sunlight is not right-angled. With one side and all the angles known, the sine rule finds the other sides.

solution.label: a
steps: (i) A vertical tree would make \(90^\circ\) with the ground. This one leans \(8^\circ\) towards S, so the angle on that side is \(90^\circ - 8^\circ = 82^\circ\).
(ii) The angles of triangle BST add up to \(180^\circ\): \(180^\circ - 40^\circ - 82^\circ = 58^\circ\).

solution.label: b
steps: BT is opposite the \(40^\circ\) angle and BS is opposite the \(58^\circ\) angle.
Sine rule: \(\dfrac{\mathrm{BT}}{\sin 40^\circ} = \dfrac{12}{\sin 58^\circ}\)
\(\mathrm{BT} = \dfrac{12\sin 40^\circ}{\sin 58^\circ} = 9.095\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: The tree is \(8^\circ\) from the vertical, so the vertical height is \(\mathrm{BT} \times \cos 8^\circ\).
\(9.095\ldots \times \cos 8^\circ = 9.007\ldots\)

stem: In this question, give each bearing to the nearest degree.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the size of angle \(\mathrm{B\hat{A}C}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down the bearing of C from A.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the bearing of A from C.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the bearing of C from B.

idea: Three sides are known, so the cosine rule gives the angles. Because B is due north of A, the line AB is itself a north line, and each angle of the triangle can be turned into a bearing.

solution.label: a
steps: The angle at A is opposite BC.
\(\mathrm{B\hat{A}C} = 83.95\ldots^\circ\)

solution.label: b
steps: At A, north is the direction of B. The bearing of C is the angle turned clockwise from AB to AC, which is the angle found in part (a).

solution.label: c
steps: This is the opposite direction: \(83.95\ldots^\circ + 180^\circ = 263.95\ldots^\circ\)

solution.label: d
steps: First find the angle at B: \(\cos(\mathrm{A\hat{B}C}) = \dfrac{2.4^{2} + 2.9^{2} - 1.9^{2}}{2 \times 2.4 \times 2.9} = \dfrac{10.56}{13.92} = 0.7586\ldots\), so \(\mathrm{A\hat{B}C} = 40.65\ldots^\circ\)
At B, the direction to A is south, a bearing of \(180^\circ\). C is to the east, so turn back from south towards east by \(40.65\ldots^\circ\).
\(180^\circ - 40.65\ldots^\circ = 139.3\ldots^\circ\)

\(\mathrm{T\hat{H}B} = 23.78\ldots^\circ\) The angle at H is acute, because it is opposite a side that is not the longest.

stem: \(\mathrm{OA} = 62\) m, \(\mathrm{OB} = 48\) m, \(\mathrm{OC} = 55\) m, \(\mathrm{OD} = 70\) m, \(\mathrm{A\hat{O}B} = 85^\circ\), \(\mathrm{B\hat{O}C} = 110^\circ\) and \(\mathrm{C\hat{O}D} = 75^\circ\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the size of angle \(\mathrm{D\hat{O}A}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the field.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the length of the side [AB].

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the perimeter of the field.

parts.label: e
parts.text: A straight fence is going to be built across the field from A to C. Find the length of the fence.

idea: The lines from O cut the field into four triangles. In each one, two sides and the angle between them are known. That is exactly what is needed for the area formula \(\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C\) and for the cosine rule.

solution.label: a
steps: The four angles at O make a full turn: \(360^\circ - 85^\circ - 110^\circ - 75^\circ\).

solution.label: b
steps: Triangle AOB: \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 62 \times 48 \times \sin 85^\circ = 1482.3\ldots\)
Triangle BOC: \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 48 \times 55 \times \sin 110^\circ = 1240.3\ldots\)
Triangle COD: \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 55 \times 70 \times \sin 75^\circ = 1859.4\ldots\)
Triangle DOA: \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 70 \times 62 \times \sin 90^\circ = 2170\)

solution.label: c
steps: Cosine rule in triangle AOB: \(\mathrm{AB}^{2} = 62^{2} + 48^{2} - 2 \times 62 \times 48 \times \cos 85^\circ = 5629.2\ldots\)
\(\mathrm{AB} = 75.02\ldots\)

solution.label: d
steps: Use the cosine rule in the same way in the other three triangles.
\(\mathrm{BC} = \sqrt{48^{2} + 55^{2} - 2 \times 48 \times 55 \times \cos 110^\circ} = 84.46\ldots\)
\(\mathrm{CD} = \sqrt{55^{2} + 70^{2} - 2 \times 55 \times 70 \times \cos 75^\circ} = 77.02\ldots\)
\(\mathrm{DA} = \sqrt{70^{2} + 62^{2}} = 93.50\ldots\) (the angle at O is \(90^\circ\), so this is Pythagoras).
Perimeter: \(75.02\ldots + 84.46\ldots + 77.02\ldots + 93.50\ldots = 330.0\ldots\)

solution.label: e
steps: Use triangle AOC. Going from OA to OC through B turns \(85^\circ + 110^\circ = 195^\circ\), which is more than a half-turn. The angle inside triangle AOC is the rest of the full turn: \(360^\circ - 195^\circ = 165^\circ\).
\(\mathrm{AC}^{2} = 62^{2} + 55^{2} - 2 \times 62 \times 55 \times \cos 165^\circ = 13\,456.6\ldots\)
\(\mathrm{AC} = 116.0\ldots\) The fence passes close to O but not through it, so it is a little shorter than \(62 + 55 = 117\) m.

parts.label: e
parts.text: The diagonals of a parallelogram cut each other in half. Find the acute angle between the two diagonals.

idea: A diagonal cuts a parallelogram into two equal triangles. Each diagonal is the third side of a triangle in which two sides and the angle between them are known, so the cosine rule finds it. The two diagonals are different because the angles they are opposite are different.

solution.label: a
steps: Neighbouring angles of a parallelogram add up to \(180^\circ\): \(180^\circ - 75^\circ\).

solution.label: b
steps: In triangle ABD the angle at A is \(75^\circ\): \(\mathrm{BD}^{2} = 40^{2} + 25^{2} - 2 \times 40 \times 25 \times \cos 75^\circ = 1707.3\ldots\)
\(\mathrm{BD} = 41.32\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: In triangle ABC, \(\mathrm{BC} = \mathrm{AD} = 25\) and the angle at B is \(105^\circ\): \(\mathrm{AC}^{2} = 40^{2} + 25^{2} - 2 \times 40 \times 25 \times \cos 105^\circ = 2742.6\ldots\)
\(\mathrm{AC} = 52.37\ldots\)

solution.label: d
steps: The parallelogram is two copies of triangle ABD: \(2 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 25 \times \sin 75^\circ = 965.9\ldots\)

solution.label: e
steps: Let the diagonals cross at X. Then \(\mathrm{AX} = \dfrac{52.37\ldots}{2} = 26.18\ldots\) and \(\mathrm{BX} = \dfrac{41.32\ldots}{2} = 20.66\ldots\)
Cosine rule in triangle AXB, where \(\mathrm{AB} = 40\): \(\cos(\mathrm{A\hat{X}B}) = \dfrac{(26.18\ldots)^{2} + (20.66\ldots)^{2} - 40^{2}}{2 \times 26.18\ldots \times 20.66\ldots} = -0.4505\ldots\)
\(\mathrm{A\hat{X}B} = 116.7\ldots^\circ\) This is obtuse, so the acute angle between the diagonals is \(180^\circ - 116.7\ldots^\circ = 63.22\ldots^\circ\)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the size of angle \(\mathrm{A\hat{F}B}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the distance AF.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the height of the hill, FS.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the angle of elevation of S from B.

idea: Work in one flat triangle at a time. The triangle on the ground, ABF, has no right angle, so it needs the sine rule. The triangles that stand upright, AFS and BFS, each have a right angle at F.

solution.label: b
steps: In triangle ABF, AF is opposite the \(73^\circ\) angle and AB is opposite the \(43^\circ\) angle.
Sine rule: \(\dfrac{\mathrm{AF}}{\sin 73^\circ} = \dfrac{400}{\sin 43^\circ}\)
\(\mathrm{AF} = \dfrac{400\sin 73^\circ}{\sin 43^\circ} = 560.8\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: Triangle AFS has a right angle at F and an angle of \(23^\circ\) at A.
\(\mathrm{FS} = 560.8\ldots \times \tan 23^\circ = 238.0\ldots\)

solution.label: d
steps: First find BF with the sine rule: \(\mathrm{BF} = \dfrac{400\sin 64^\circ}{\sin 43^\circ} = 527.1\ldots\)
Triangle BFS has a right angle at F: \(\tan(\mathrm{F\hat{B}S}) = \dfrac{238.0\ldots}{527.1\ldots} = 0.4516\ldots\)
\(\mathrm{F\hat{B}S} = 24.30\ldots^\circ\) B is nearer to F than A is, so the summit looks higher from B.

stem: The bend at each end of a running track is a semicircle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In lane 1 the radius of the bend is 36.5 m. Find the length of the bend in lane 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In lane 8 the bend is 142 m long. Find the radius of the bend in lane 8.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A runner in lane 1 starts at the beginning of the bend and runs 30 m round it. Find the angle that she has turned through, measured at the centre of the semicircle.

idea: The length of an arc is a fraction of the circumference of the whole circle. The fraction is the angle of the arc divided by \(360^\circ\), and a semicircle is exactly half.

solution.label: a
steps: Half of the circumference: \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 2\pi \times 36.5 = 114.6\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: Arc length \(= \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r\), so \(30 = \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi \times 36.5\).
\(\theta = \dfrac{30 \times 360}{2\pi \times 36.5} = 47.09\ldots\)

stem: A pie chart of radius 6 cm shows how the 150 students in a year group travel to school. The sector for students who walk has an angle of \(96^\circ\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the area of the sector for students who walk.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the length of the arc of this sector.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The arc of the sector for students who travel by bus is 11 cm long. Find the angle of this sector.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the number of students who walk to school.

idea: A sector is a fraction of a circle, and the fraction is its angle divided by \(360^\circ\). The same fraction applies to the area, to the arc length and, in a pie chart, to the number of people.

solution.label: a
steps: \(\dfrac{96}{360} \times \pi \times 6^{2} = 30.15\ldots\)

solution.label: b
steps: \(\dfrac{96}{360} \times 2\pi \times 6 = 10.05\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: The whole circumference is \(2\pi \times 6 = 12\pi\) cm, and the arc is 11 cm of it.
\(\theta = \dfrac{11}{12\pi} \times 360 = 105.0\ldots\)

stem: The Earth can be modelled as a sphere of radius 6371 km. The latitude of a place is the angle, measured at the centre of the Earth, between that place and the equator. The city P is on the equator. The city Q is due north of P, at a latitude of \(41^\circ\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the distance from P to Q, measured along the surface of the Earth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The city R is 2500 km due north of P, measured along the surface. Find the latitude of R.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The Earth turns once every 24 hours. Find the speed, in km per hour, at which a point on the equator is carried round by this rotation.

idea: A journey due north follows an arc of a circle whose centre is the centre of the Earth and whose radius is the radius of the Earth. The angle of the arc is the change in latitude.

solution.label: a
steps: The arc PQ has angle \(41^\circ\) at the centre of the Earth.
\(\dfrac{41}{360} \times 2\pi \times 6371 = 4558.9\ldots\)

solution.label: b
steps: \(\dfrac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi \times 6371 = 2500\)
\(\theta = \dfrac{2500 \times 360}{2\pi \times 6371} = 22.48\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: In 24 hours a point on the equator travels once round the Earth: \(2\pi \times 6371 = 40\,030.1\ldots\) km.

stem: A vinyl record turns at a steady rate of \(33\tfrac{1}{3}\) revolutions per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the record turns through \(200^\circ\) each second.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A point on the edge of the record is 15 cm from the centre. Find the distance that this point travels in one second.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the distance travelled in one second by a point that is 6 cm from the centre.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the time that the point on the edge takes to travel 10 metres.

idea: Every point on a turning disc moves through the same angle in the same time. Each point travels along an arc, and the length of the arc depends on how far the point is from the centre.

solution.label: a
steps: In one minute the record turns through \(33\tfrac{1}{3} \times 360^\circ = 12\,000^\circ\).
In one second: \(12\,000^\circ \div 60 = 200^\circ\).

solution.label: b
steps: The point moves along an arc of radius 15 cm and angle \(200^\circ\): \(\dfrac{200}{360} \times 2\pi \times 15 = 52.35\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: Same angle, smaller radius: \(\dfrac{200}{360} \times 2\pi \times 6 = 20.94\ldots\)

solution.label: d
steps: \(10\) m \(= 1000\) cm, and the point covers \(52.35\ldots\) cm each second.

parts.text: By using triangle OMB, show that \(r = 29\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the size of angle \(\mathrm{A\hat{O}B}\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the length of the beam.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the area of the region between the beam and the straight line [AB].

parts.label: e
parts.text: A second beam is also an arc of a circle. Its ends are 40 m apart at the same height, and its highest point is 10 m above the midpoint of the line joining its ends. Find the radius of this arc.

idea: A line from the centre of a circle to the midpoint of a chord meets the chord at a right angle. This gives a right-angled triangle that links the radius to the width and the height of an arch.

solution.label: a
steps: N is on the circle, so \(\mathrm{ON} = r\). M is 8 m below N, so \(\mathrm{OM} = r - 8\). Also \(\mathrm{MB} = 20\) and \(\mathrm{OB} = r\).
Triangle OMB has a right angle at M: \(r^{2} = 20^{2} + (r - 8)^{2}\)

solution.label: b
steps: In triangle OMB, \(\sin(\mathrm{M\hat{O}B}) = \dfrac{20}{29}\), so \(\mathrm{M\hat{O}B} = 43.60\ldots^\circ\)
\(\mathrm{A\hat{O}B}\) is twice this: \(87.20\ldots^\circ\)

solution.label: c
steps: Arc length \(= \dfrac{87.20\ldots}{360} \times 2\pi \times 29 = 44.13\ldots\)

solution.label: d
steps: The region is the sector AOB with triangle AOB removed.
Sector: \(\dfrac{87.20\ldots}{360} \times \pi \times 29^{2} = 640.0\ldots\)
Triangle AOB has base 40 m and height \(\mathrm{OM} = 29 - 8 = 21\) m: \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 21 = 420\)

solution.label: e
steps: Use the method of part (a) with 10 in place of 8. The centre is now \(R - 10\) below the midpoint of the chord, where \(R\) is the new radius.
\(20R = 500\), so \(R = 25\). A taller arch over the same width is part of a smaller circle.

stem: A measuring wheel is used to measure distances along the ground. It is a circle of diameter 35 cm, and it rolls along the ground without slipping.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of complete turns that the wheel makes when it is pushed along a path that is 400 m long.
A point P on the rim of the wheel is touching the ground. The wheel is then pushed forwards.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the distance that the wheel moves forwards as it turns through \(250^\circ\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the height of P above the ground when the wheel has turned through \(250^\circ\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the angle that the wheel has turned through when P is first 26.25 cm above the ground.

idea: When a wheel rolls without slipping, the distance it moves along the ground is equal to the length of the arc that has touched the ground. One full turn moves it forward by one circumference.

solution.label: a
steps: One turn moves the wheel one circumference: \(\pi \times 35 = 109.9\ldots\) cm.
The question asks for complete turns, so round down.

solution.label: b
steps: The wheel moves forward by the length of an arc of \(250^\circ\): \(\dfrac{250}{360} \times \pi \times 35 = 76.35\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: The centre of the wheel is always \(17.5\) cm above the ground. P starts directly below the centre.
After a turn of \(\theta\), P is \(17.5\cos\theta\) below the centre, so its height is \(17.5 - 17.5\cos\theta\).
For \(\theta = 250^\circ\): \(17.5\cos 250^\circ = -5.985\ldots\), which is negative because P is now above the centre. Height \(= 17.5 + 5.985\ldots = 23.48\ldots\)

solution.label: d
steps: The first angle with this cosine is \(\theta = 120^\circ\).

stem: Two villages are at \(\mathrm{A}(1,\,2)\) and \(\mathrm{B}(7,\,6)\) on a map, where 1 unit represents 1 km. A straight road, \(L\), has equation \(y = -1.5x + 10\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the coordinates of M, the midpoint of [AB].

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that M lies on \(L\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the gradient of the line through A and B.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Show that \(L\) is perpendicular to the line through A and B.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Parts (b) and (d) show that \(L\) is the perpendicular bisector of [AB]. The point \(\mathrm{P}(6,\,1)\) is on the road. Find the distance from P to each village.

idea: The perpendicular bisector of a line segment passes through its midpoint and meets it at a right angle. Every point on the perpendicular bisector is the same distance from the two ends of the segment.

solution.label: a
steps: Average the coordinates: \(\left(\dfrac{1 + 7}{2},\ \dfrac{2 + 6}{2}\right)\)

solution.label: b
steps: Put \(x = 4\) into the equation of \(L\): \(y = -1.5 \times 4 + 10 = 4\). This is the \(y\)-coordinate of M.

solution.label: d
steps: The gradient of \(L\) is \(-1.5\). Multiply the two gradients: \(-1.5 \times \dfrac{2}{3} = -1\). A product of \(-1\) means that the lines are perpendicular.

solution.label: e
steps: The two distances are equal, as they must be for any point on the perpendicular bisector.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the school that a child who lives at \((6,\,1)\) goes to.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A child lives at \((3,\,7)\), which is on an edge of the diagram. Write down the two schools that are equally near to this child's home.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write down the equation of the edge between the cell of A and the cell of B.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the distance from V to school A.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Write down the distance from V to school C.

idea: In a Voronoi diagram, every point inside a cell is nearer to that cell's site than to any other site. A point on an edge is equally near to two sites, and a vertex is equally near to three.

solution.label: a
steps: The point \((6,\,1)\) is to the right of the vertical edge and below the edge that runs from V to \((10,\,6)\), so it is in the cell of B.

solution.label: b
steps: The point \((3,\,7)\) is on the edge that runs from V to \((0,\,10)\). This edge separates the cell of A from the cell of C.

solution.label: c
steps: The edge is the vertical line through V, halfway between \(x = 2\) and \(x = 8\).

solution.label: e
steps: A vertex is the same distance from each of the three sites around it. Check: \(\sqrt{(7 - 5)^{2} + (8 - 5)^{2}} = \sqrt{13}\).

stem: A city has three bicycle hire stations, at \(\mathrm{P}(2,\,1)\), \(\mathrm{Q}(8,\,1)\) and \(\mathrm{R}(2,\,7)\), where 1 unit represents 1 km.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the equation of the perpendicular bisector of [PQ].

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down the equation of the perpendicular bisector of [PR].

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write down the coordinates of the point V that is the same distance from all three stations.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the distance from V to each station.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of [QR].

idea: The perpendicular bisector of a horizontal segment is a vertical line through its midpoint, and the other way round. The point where two perpendicular bisectors cross is the same distance from all three sites, so the third perpendicular bisector passes through it too.

solution.label: a
steps: [PQ] is horizontal, from \(x = 2\) to \(x = 8\). Its perpendicular bisector is the vertical line through the middle.

solution.label: b
steps: [PR] is vertical, from \(y = 1\) to \(y = 7\). Its perpendicular bisector is the horizontal line through the middle.

solution.label: c
steps: A point on \(x = 5\) is equally far from P and Q. A point on \(y = 4\) is equally far from P and R. The point on both lines is equally far from all three.

solution.label: e
steps: The gradient of QR is \(\dfrac{7 - 1}{2 - 8} = -1\), so the perpendicular gradient is \(1\).
The midpoint of [QR] is \((5,\,4)\), which is V. The line with gradient 1 through \((5,\,4)\) is \(y - 4 = x - 5\).

stem: Three mountain huts are at \(\mathrm{A}(2,\,0)\), \(\mathrm{B}(10,\,4)\) and \(\mathrm{C}(1,\,7)\), where 1 unit represents 1 km.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of [AB]. Give your answer in the form \(y = mx + c\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the point \(\mathrm{V}(5,\,4)\) lies on this perpendicular bisector.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that V is the same distance from A as it is from C.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State what parts (b) and (c) show about the distances from V to the three huts.

parts.label: e
parts.text: A walker is at \(\mathrm{W}(6,\,5)\). Determine which hut is nearest to the walker.

idea: To find a perpendicular bisector you need two things: the midpoint of the segment, and the gradient that is perpendicular to the segment. Any point on the perpendicular bisector of [AB] is the same distance from A as from B.

solution.label: a
steps: Midpoint of [AB]: \(\left(\dfrac{2 + 10}{2},\ \dfrac{0 + 4}{2}\right) = (6,\,2)\)
Gradient of AB: \(\dfrac{4 - 0}{10 - 2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\). The perpendicular gradient is \(-2\).

solution.label: b
steps: Put \(x = 5\) into the equation: \(y = -2 \times 5 + 14 = 4\). This is the \(y\)-coordinate of V.
solution.answer: When \(x = 5\), \(y = 4\), so V is on the line

solution.label: d
steps: V is on the perpendicular bisector of [AB], so \(\mathrm{VA} = \mathrm{VB}\). Part (c) shows that \(\mathrm{VA} = \mathrm{VC}\).
So all three distances are equal. In the Voronoi diagram for the three huts, V is the vertex where the three cells meet.
solution.answer: V is the same distance, 5 km, from all three huts

solution.label: e
solution.answer: Hut B, which is 4.12 km away

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use nearest neighbour interpolation to estimate the amount of nitrogen in the soil at the point \((3,\,7)\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The point \((4,\,7)\) lies on an edge of the diagram. Explain why nearest neighbour interpolation does not give a single estimate at this point, and write down the two values that it could give.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the area of the cell that contains Q. Give your answer in m\(^2\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Fertiliser is spread over the whole of the cell that contains Q, at 30 grams per m\(^2\). Find the mass of fertiliser that is needed, in kilograms.

idea: Nearest neighbour interpolation gives every point the value measured at the nearest site. That is the same as giving every point in a cell the value at that cell's site.

solution.label: a
steps: The point \((3,\,7)\) is in the cell on the left, which contains P. Check: it is \(\sqrt{1^{2} + 2^{2}} = \sqrt{5}\) from P and \(\sqrt{3^{2} + 2^{2}} = \sqrt{13}\) from R.

solution.label: b
steps: The point \((4,\,7)\) is on the edge between the cell of P and the cell of R, so it is the same distance from P as from R (both distances are \(\sqrt{8}\)).
There is no single nearest site.
solution.answer: P and R are equally near, so the estimate could be 12 or 9 mg per kg

solution.label: c
steps: The cell of Q is the triangle with vertices \((1,\,0)\), \((11,\,0)\) and \((6,\,5)\). Its base is 10 units and its height is 5 units: area \(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 5 = 25\) square units.
One unit is 20 m, so one square unit is \(20 \times 20 = 400\) m\(^2\).

stem: The beekeeper wants to add a fifth hive. It must be at a vertex of the diagram, and as far as possible from the hive that is nearest to it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the three hives that are nearest to \(\mathrm{V_2}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the distance, in metres, from \(\mathrm{V_1}\) to hive A.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the distance, in metres, from \(\mathrm{V_2}\) to hive C.

parts.label: d
parts.text: \(\mathrm{V_1}\) is in the middle of a pond, so a hive cannot be put there. State where the new hive should be put, and write down its distance from the nearest hive.

idea: The point that is furthest from every site is always at a vertex of the Voronoi diagram, because a vertex is where the distance to the three nearest sites is as large as it can be. Compare the vertices and choose the one with the greatest distance to its sites.

solution.label: a
steps: \(\mathrm{V_2}\) is where three cells meet: the cells of B, C and D. These are its three nearest hives, and they are all the same distance from it.

solution.label: b
steps: One unit is 10 m: \(3.162\ldots \times 10 = 31.62\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: C is directly above \(\mathrm{V_2}\): \(7 - 4.5 = 2.5\) units.

solution.label: d
steps: \(\mathrm{V_1}\) is further from its nearest hives (31.6 m) than \(\mathrm{V_2}\) is (25 m), so it would be the best place. It cannot be used.
The only other vertex is \(\mathrm{V_2}\).
solution.answer: At \(\mathrm{V_2}(7,\,4.5)\), which is 25 m from the nearest hives

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that this perpendicular bisector meets the southern edge of the town, \(y = 0\), at the point \((3.125,\,0)\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the point where this perpendicular bisector meets the line \(y = 3\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: The cell of E is a hexagon. It is symmetrical about the line \(x = 4\) and about the line \(y = 3\). Find the area of the cell of E.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Write down the fraction of the town in which E is the nearest station.

idea: The cell of a site is the region that is on the site's own side of every perpendicular bisector between it and its neighbours. Here the four bisectors are mirror images of each other, so one of them is enough to find the whole cell.

solution.label: a
steps: Midpoint of [AE]: \((2,\,1.5)\). Gradient of AE: \(\dfrac{3}{4}\). The perpendicular gradient is \(-\dfrac{4}{3}\).
Multiply by 3: \(3y - 4.5 = -4x + 8\), so \(4x + 3y = 12.5\). Double it to make every number an integer.

solution.label: d
steps: The edge between A and E runs from \((3.125,\,0)\) to \((0.875,\,3)\). Reflect these points in \(x = 4\) and in \(y = 3\) to get the other corners of the hexagon: \((4.875,\,0)\), \((7.125,\,3)\), \((4.875,\,6)\) and \((3.125,\,6)\).
The line \(y = 3\) cuts the hexagon into two equal trapezia. The lower one has parallel sides \(4.875 - 3.125 = 1.75\) and \(7.125 - 0.875 = 6.25\), and height 3.
Area of one trapezium: \(\dfrac{1}{2}(1.75 + 6.25) \times 3 = 12\). The hexagon is two of these.

solution.label: e
steps: The town has area \(8 \times 6 = 48\) km\(^2\), and \(\dfrac{24}{48} = \dfrac{1}{2}\). One station out of five serves half of the town, because it is in the middle.

The fourth post, D, is not shown. The edge between the cell of A and the cell of D lies on the line \(y = 2x - 7\).

parts.label: e

idea: An edge of a Voronoi diagram is part of the perpendicular bisector of the two sites on either side of it. So the line joining the two sites is perpendicular to the edge, and the edge passes through the midpoint of the two sites. Working backwards from the edge gives a missing site.

solution.label: a
steps: The edge has gradient 2. The line AD is perpendicular to it, so its gradient is \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\), because \(2 \times -\dfrac{1}{2} = -1\).

solution.label: b
steps: The line has gradient \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\) and passes through \(\mathrm{A}(7,\,2)\): \(y - 2 = -\dfrac{1}{2}(x - 7)\)

solution.label: d
steps: M is the midpoint of [AD]. From A to M the coordinates change by \(-2\) and \(+1\).
Make the same changes again, starting from M: \((5 - 2,\ 3 + 1)\).

solution.label: e
solution.answer: Both distances are \(\sqrt{10} = 3.16\) units, so they are equal

solution.label: f
steps: This edge is part of the perpendicular bisector of [BD], with \(\mathrm{B}(9,\,6)\) and \(\mathrm{D}(3,\,4)\).
Midpoint: \(\left(\dfrac{9 + 3}{2},\ \dfrac{6 + 4}{2}\right) = (6,\,5)\). This is the vertex in part (e), as it should be: the vertex is on every edge that meets there.
Gradient of BD: \(\dfrac{6 - 4}{9 - 3} = \dfrac{1}{3}\). The perpendicular gradient is \(-3\).

stem: An aircraft flies in a straight line along the path \(y = 0.5x + 3\), from \((0,\,3)\) to \((10,\,8)\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the edge between the cell of A and the cell of C lies on the line \(y = x + 2\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The edge between the cell of B and the cell of C lies on the line \(y = -x + 12\). Find the coordinates of the vertex V.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the point where control of the aircraft passes from A to C.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the point where control of the aircraft passes from C to B.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the distance, in kilometres, that the aircraft flies while it is controlled by C.

parts.label: f
parts.text: The aircraft flies at 900 km per hour. Find the time, in minutes, for which it is controlled by C.

idea: Control changes at the moment the aircraft crosses an edge of the Voronoi diagram. Each crossing point is where the flight path meets the line that the edge lies on, so it is found by solving two equations together.

solution.label: a
steps: The edge is part of the perpendicular bisector of [AC].
Midpoint of [AC]: \(\left(\dfrac{1 + 5}{2},\ \dfrac{7 + 3}{2}\right) = (3,\,5)\)
Gradient of AC: \(\dfrac{3 - 7}{5 - 1} = -1\). The perpendicular gradient is \(1\).
solution.answer: Midpoint \((3,\,5)\) and gradient 1 give \(y = x + 2\), as required

solution.label: b
steps: V is on both edges: \(x + 2 = -x + 12\), so \(2x = 10\) and \(x = 5\). Then \(y = 5 + 2 = 7\).

solution.label: c
steps: The aircraft starts in the cell of A. It leaves this cell where its path meets \(y = x + 2\).

solution.label: e
steps: One unit is 100 km: \(447.2\ldots\) km.

solution.label: f
steps: Time \(= \dfrac{447.2\ldots}{900}\) hours. Multiply by 60 to change to minutes: \(29.81\ldots\)
